chunks.title: Orbit axes & the recti
chunks.tldr: Orbital axis is 23° from the visual axis. MR/LR = pure horizontal. SR: elevate + adduct + intort; IR: depress + adduct + extort. Test vertical recti in abduction (23°). Spiral of Tillaux: MR 5.5, IR 6.5, LR 6.9, SR 7.7 mm.
points: Orbital walls 45° apart → axis 22.5° (~23°).
Fick axes: Z vertical (left/right), X horizontal (up/down), Y front-back (torsion). Listing plane = coronal through rotation centre.
Intorsion = superior limbus rotates nasally.
All recti from the annulus of Zinn.
SR/IR in 23° abduction = pure elevator/depressor. In 67° adduction (theoretical) = pure torsion.
Pulleys near the equator are the functional origins; displaced pulleys → A/V patterns, sagging eye.
chunks.hook: Tillaux from MR clockwise-ish: '5.5, 6.5, 6.9, 7.7 — Mighty Irish Lads Swim'. RAD SIN: Recti ADduct; Superiors INtort.

cards.q: Best gaze position to test superior rectus?
cards.a: Abduction (about 23°) – it then acts purely as an elevator.

cards.q: Which rectus inserts closest to the limbus?
cards.a: Medial rectus (5.5 mm).

chunks.title: Obliques & innervation
chunks.tldr: Obliques insert behind the equator, 51° to visual axis. SO: intort + depress + abduct; test in adduction (pure depressor). IO: extort + elevate + abduct; test in adduction. Nerves: LR6 SO4, rest III.
points: SO: from above optic foramen → trochlea → back to posterior upper temporal globe.
SO anterior fibres = intorsion, posterior fibres = depression (Harada–Ito targets the anterior fibres).
SO palsy shows mainly as poor depression in adduction.
IO: from orbital floor lateral to lacrimal sac → inserts posterior lower temporal near the macula.
In 39° abduction obliques act mainly as torters.
III also supplies levator, sphincter pupillae, ciliary muscle.
chunks.hook: LR6 SO4 (the rest are 3). Obliques ABduct ('RAD SIN' + obliques the opposite).

cards.q: Primary action of the superior oblique?
cards.a: Intorsion (secondary: depression, abduction).

cards.q: Where is SO weakness most evident?
cards.a: Failure of depression in adduction.

chunks.title: Ductions, versions, vergences & AC/A
chunks.tldr: Duction = one eye. Version = both same way. Vergence = opposite ways. Convergence parts: tonic, proximal, fusional, accommodative. Normal AC/A = 3–5 Δ/D.
points: Secondary positions: straight up/down/left/right. Tertiary: oblique positions.
Head tilt right → RE intorts, LE extorts (righting reflex).
Fusional convergence driven by bitemporal disparity.
Near triad: accommodation + convergence + miosis.
6 cardinal positions (one muscle per eye mainly responsible); 9 diagnostic positions.
chunks.hook: Vergence = Very different directions.

cards.q: Normal AC/A ratio?
cards.a: 3–5 prism dioptres per dioptre of accommodation.

cards.q: Yoke muscle of the left superior oblique?
cards.a: Right inferior rectus.

chunks.title: Hering & Sherrington laws
chunks.tldr: Sherrington: agonist contracts → its antagonist relaxes (same eye). Hering: yoke muscles get equal innervation. So in a palsy, secondary deviation (paretic eye fixing) > primary deviation.
points: Agonist–antagonist (same eye, opposite). Synergists (same eye, same direction). Yokes (one in each eye, same direction).
L LR palsy, R fixing → L eye esotropic (primary deviation).
L fixing → extra drive to L LR → equal extra to R MR → bigger deviation (secondary).
Muscle sequelae (e.g. L SO palsy): 1) L SO underacts → 2) R IR (yoke) overacts → 3) L IO (antagonist) overacts/contracts → 4) R SR (contralateral antagonist) inhibitional palsy.
Over time a palsy spreads → becomes comitant; hard to find the original muscle.
chunks.hook: Hering = Hers + His get equal (both eyes). Sherrington = Same eye, see-saw.

cards.q: In a paretic squint, which is larger: primary or secondary deviation?
cards.a: Secondary (paretic eye fixing).

cards.q: State Sherrington's law.
cards.a: Increased innervation to a muscle is accompanied by reciprocal decreased innervation to its antagonist.

chunks.title: BSV, horopter & Panum's area
chunks.tldr: BSV needs normal retinal correspondence. Horopter: points seen single. Panum's area: small disparity → single + stereopsis; outside → physiological diplopia. Grades: SP → fusion → stereopsis.
points: Nasal retina projects to temporal field (and vice versa).
Retinomotor value: 0 at fovea, increases outward (guides saccade size).
Panum's area shallow at fixation (~6 arc sec), deeper peripherally.
Sensory fusion (central or peripheral) vs motor fusion (vergence).
Peripheral fusion needed for BSV (lost in advanced glaucoma/pituitary field loss).
Fusional amplitudes: convergence 15–20 Δ distance / 25 Δ near; divergence 6–10 / 12–14 Δ; vertical 2–3 Δ; cyclo ~8°.
chunks.hook: On horopter = single flat. In Panum = single 3D. Outside = double.

cards.q: What is Panum's fusional area?
cards.a: Zone around the horopter where slightly disparate images are still fused, producing stereopsis.

cards.q: Normal fusional convergence amplitude for near?
cards.a: About 25 prism dioptres.

chunks.title: Diplopia, confusion, suppression & ARC
chunks.tldr: New squint → confusion (two objects on two foveae) + diplopia. Kids (<6–8 yrs) adapt: suppression (→ amblyopia if constant, one eye) or ARC (fovea paired with non-fovea, typical in microtropia). Eso = uncrossed diplopia; exo = crossed.
points: Suppression: central (stops confusion) vs peripheral (stops diplopia); monocular vs alternating; facultative (only when deviated, e.g. intermittent XT, Duane) vs obligatory.
ARC = positive adaptation; best in small stable angles.
Head posture: turn head towards the weak muscle's field ('head goes where the eye can't').
R SO weakness → head tilt to left, face turn left, chin down.
Losing a childhood head posture may mean losing BSV → surgery.
chunks.hook: ESO = Same Side (uncrossed). eXo = X (crossed).

cards.q: Type of diplopia in esotropia?
cards.a: Uncrossed (homonymous).

cards.q: Head tilt in a right fourth nerve palsy?
cards.a: To the left (away from the affected side).

chunks.title: Amblyopia: types & treatment
chunks.tldr: Reduced best-corrected VA (≥2 lines difference) with no eye disease. Types: strabismic, anisometropic (≥1 D), deprivation, bilateral ametropic, meridional. Treat: glasses → patching or atropine penalisation. Window to ~7–8 yrs (longer for aniso).
points: Crowding: amblyopes read single letters better than rows → use crowded logMAR tests.
Always look at the fundus first (exclude organic disease).
Patching: faster; younger = quicker but risk of occlusion amblyopia → check both eyes.
No gain after 6 months of good patching → stop.
Atropine: best for mild–moderate (≥6/24), hyperopic aniso; hard to cheat; weekend dosing may work.
Compliance is the biggest barrier.
chunks.hook: Glasses first, then patch, then pupil-blur.

cards.q: Anisometropia of how much can cause amblyopia?
cards.a: As little as 1 dioptre.

cards.q: What is the crowding phenomenon?
cards.a: VA is better with single optotypes than with letters in a row – exaggerated in amblyopia.

chunks.title: Testing vision in children
chunks.tldr: Preverbal: fix & follow, objection to occlusion, fixation preference, 10 Δ test, rotation test, preferential looking (Teller, Keeler, Cardiff). Age 2: Kay pictures. Age 3: Keeler logMAR / Sonksen matching. Test at 3–4 m.
points: Fixation held through a blink → good VA; alternates → equal.
Rotation test: post-rotatory nystagmus persists if vision is poor.
Grating acuity (Teller) overestimates VA in amblyopia.
Crowded recognition tests are needed to diagnose amblyopia.
chunks.hook: 2 = pictures (Kay), 3 = letters (Keeler/Sonksen).

cards.q: Why can Teller cards miss amblyopia?
cards.a: Grating (resolution) acuity often exceeds recognition acuity in amblyopes.

chunks.title: Stereo tests
chunks.tldr: Lower arc-seconds = better. Normal ~60″. Titmus: fly 3000″, animals 400–100″, circles 800–40″ (polarised). TNO: random dot, red-green, 480–15″. Frisby: plates, no glasses, 600–15″. Lang: no glasses, 1200–200″.
points: Random dot (TNO, Frisby) = best proof of real BSV.
Contour tests (Titmus) better if weak/ARC binocularity.
All at ~40 cm (Frisby: measure distance).
Lang star is visible monocularly (attention grabber).
chunks.hook: Fly = 3000 (giant). TNO = 15 (tiny).

cards.q: Stereo value of the Titmus fly?
cards.a: About 3000 seconds of arc (gross stereopsis).

chunks.title: Worth 4-dot, Bagolini & 4Δ test
chunks.tldr: Worth 4-dot (green RE, red LE): 4 = BSV (or harmonious ARC if squint); 2 red = R suppression; 3 green = L suppression; 5 = diplopia. Bagolini: X = BSV/ARC. 4 Δ base-out: no movement → central suppression scotoma (microtropia). 20 Δ base-out: fusion in infants.
points: Results only make sense if you know whether a squint is present.
Worth alternating red/green = alternating suppression.
Bagolini: two lines not crossing = diplopia; one line = suppression; gap = central scotoma.
20 Δ base-out: most children with BSV overcome by 6 months.
Convergence to target from 3–4 months.
chunks.hook: Green on Right, red on Left. You see the colour of the eye that's working: 2 red = only left eye → right suppressed.

cards.q: Worth 4-dot: patient sees 3 green lights. Interpretation?
cards.a: Left suppression (green lens is over the right eye).

cards.q: 4 Δ base-out over the deviating eye causes no movement. Meaning?
cards.a: Central suppression scotoma – microtropia/monofixation.

chunks.title: Synoptophore
chunks.tldr: Presents separate pictures to each eye at squint angle. Grades: 1 simultaneous perception (bird in cage), 2 fusion (rabbits + range), 3 stereopsis (bucket). ARC: subjective ≠ objective angle; difference = angle of anomaly.
points: +6.50 D eyepieces → optical distance ~6 m.
Measures horizontal, vertical, torsion in all gaze positions.
Harmonious ARC: objective angle = angle of anomaly (binocular responses present).
Unharmonious: objective angle exceeds angle of anomaly.
Fusion without range is useless in real life.
chunks.hook: Bird → Bunny → Bucket (SP, fusion, stereo).

cards.q: How is ARC detected on the synoptophore?
cards.a: Subjective and objective angles differ; the difference is the angle of anomaly.

chunks.title: Measuring deviation: Hirschberg to prism cover
chunks.tldr: Hirschberg: 1 mm reflex shift ≈ 7° (pupil edge 15°, limbus 45°). Krimsky: prisms over fixing eye. Cover test → tropia; uncover → phoria; alternate cover → total. Prism cover test: apex towards deviation.
points: Cover test: cover fixing eye, watch other: moves in → was exo; moves out → was eso.
Uncover: covered eye recovers inward → exophoria.
Use an accommodative target, not a light (except to start).
Prism cover: base-out for eso, base-down for hyper (over that eye); go to reversal then back.
Maddox wing: near phoria (horizontal, vertical, cyclo). Maddox rod: streak at 90° to rods; can't tell phoria from tropia. Double Maddox rod → torsion.
chunks.hook: Point the prism's nose (apex) at the squint.

cards.q: Hirschberg: reflex at the limbus means what angle?
cards.a: About 45°.

cards.q: Which test differentiates phoria from tropia?
cards.a: Cover–uncover test (Maddox rod cannot).

chunks.title: Motility, NPC, NPA & diplopia tests
chunks.tldr: Grade underaction −1 to −4, overaction +1 to +4. NPC <10 cm normal. NPA 8 cm at 20 → ~46 cm at 50. Postoperative diplopia test with prisms before surgery in non-binocular patients >7–8 yrs; positive → botulinum trial.
points: LR −4 = can't abduct past midline.
RAF rule for NPC (objective/subjective) and NPA.
Field of BSV ~45–50°; great for follow-up of palsies.
Fusional amplitudes via prism bar or synoptophore.
chunks.hook: NPC under 10, normal again.

cards.q: Normal near point of convergence?
cards.a: Closer than 10 cm.

chunks.title: Hess / Lees chart
chunks.tldr: Smaller chart = paretic eye; greatest restriction in paretic muscle's field. Larger chart = yoke overaction. Each square = 5°. Over time charts become comitant (old palsy).
points: Hess: red–green goggles; red in front of fixing eye; inner field 15°, outer 30°.
Lees: two screens + mirror.
Recent R SR palsy: R SR under, L IO over → later R IR contracture + L SO inhibitional palsy (can mislead).
3rd nerve: small chart, all under except LR; exo.
Recent R 4th: R SO under, R IO over; L IR over, L SR under; secondary > primary.
Congenital 4th: charts same size, primary = secondary deviation.
R 6th: small R chart with LR under; R eso.
chunks.hook: Small chart = Sick eye. Equal-sized charts = Old palsy.

cards.q: On a Hess chart, which eye has the paretic muscle?
cards.a: The eye with the smaller chart.

cards.q: Hess sign suggesting a congenital (long-standing) palsy?
cards.a: Charts of similar size (comitance spread), primary ≈ secondary deviation.

chunks.title: Cycloplegic refraction & what to prescribe
chunks.tldr: Cyclopentolate 0.5% (<6 m) / 1%: 2 drops 5 min apart, read at 30 min. Atropine 0.5% (<1 yr) / 1%: stronger, home use 1–3 days before. In esotropia give full cycloplegic hyperopic correction, even under 2.
points: Cyclo both eyes at once (avoid penalisation amblyopia).
Atropine toxicity: flushing, fever, restlessness → stop.
Hyperopia rises till ~6, then falls.
No squint: don't correct ≤4 D hyperopia unless near problems; >4 D give ~⅔.
Astigmatism ≥1.50 D: prescribe.
Myopia: <2 yrs ≥−5 D; 2–4 yrs ≥−3 D; older: any.
Anisometropia >1 D after age 3: full difference.
chunks.hook: Eso + hyperopia = give it ALL.

cards.q: Spectacle rule in a child with esotropia and hyperopia?
cards.a: Prescribe the full cycloplegic hypermetropic correction.

cards.q: Cyclopentolate concentration in infants under 6 months?

chunks.title: Pseudostrabismus, phorias & vergence problems
chunks.tldr: Pseudo-eso: epicanthus, narrow IPD, negative kappa (myopia). Pseudo-exo: wide IPD, large positive kappa (ROP dragged macula). Convergence insufficiency: students, remote NPC → exercises. Spasm of near reflex: eso + pseudomyopia + miosis (functional).
points: Normal positive kappa: reflex slightly nasal.
Phorias: Fresnel prisms (≤10–12 Δ split), fix refraction, orthoptics (CI), surgery if big.
Divergence insufficiency/paralysis: neuro cause; prisms.
Near reflex paresis: reading glasses + base-in prisms.
Spasm: don't correct pseudomyopia; reassure; atropine + reading add if persistent.
chunks.hook: Miosis in a 'sixth nerve palsy' = spasm of the near reflex.

cards.q: Key sign distinguishing spasm of the near reflex from 6th nerve palsy?
cards.a: Miosis (with pseudomyopia) during apparent abduction failure.

cards.q: Which angle kappa gives pseudoexotropia?
cards.a: Large positive angle kappa (e.g. temporally dragged macula in ROP).

chunks.title: Early-onset (infantile) esotropia
chunks.tldr: Before 6 months, large (>30 Δ) stable angle, alternating fixation, cross-fixation, normal refraction (+1 to +2). Associations: latent nystagmus, IO overaction, DVD (80% by 3). Operate by 12 months (latest 2 yrs).
points: Abduction present: doll's head, rotation, or patch one eye a few hours.
Latent nystagmus: fast phase towards the uncovered fixing eye.
DDx: bilateral 6th palsy, sensory eso, nystagmus blockage, Duane, Möbius, strabismus fixus.
Surgery: bilateral MR recession (≤6.5 mm) or R&R; >50 Δ add LR resection.
Goal: within 10 Δ with peripheral fusion (monofixation).
Later: IO overaction (~2 yrs), DVD, amblyopia 50%, accommodative element.
chunks.hook: Infantile ET 'big 3' extras: LN, IOOA, DVD.

cards.q: Ideal age for surgical alignment in infantile esotropia?
cards.a: By about 12 months (at latest 2 years).

cards.q: Describe DVD.
cards.a: Covered eye drifts up and extorts; on uncovering it comes down without the other eye moving down (violates Hering).

chunks.title: Accommodative esotropia
chunks.tldr: Refractive (normal AC/A, +2 to +7 D, onset 18 m–3 yrs): fully vs partially corrected by glasses. Non-refractive (high AC/A): eso at near only → executive bifocals. Surgery only for residual angle with glasses.
points: Fully accommodative: straight with glasses at all distances.
Partially accommodative: reduced but not eliminated; amblyopia common.
Convergence excess: normal accommodation, high AC/A.
Hypoaccommodative: weak accommodation (remote NPA) → over-effort.
Under 6: full cycloplegic Rx; over 8: maximum tolerated plus.
Executive bifocal line at lower pupil border; wean by early teens.
Surgery: bilateral MR recession (near > distance); Faden for convergence excess.
chunks.hook: Glasses fix it = fully. Glasses help = partially. Only near = bifocals.

cards.q: Treatment for convergence excess esotropia with high AC/A?
cards.a: Executive bifocals (or bilateral MR recession ± Faden).

cards.q: Typical age of onset of refractive accommodative esotropia?
cards.a: 18 months to 3 years.

chunks.title: Microtropia & other esotropias
chunks.tldr: Microtropia (<10 Δ, monofixation): anisometropia + mild amblyopia + ARC + central suppression scotoma + reduced stereo. Other ETs: near, distance (myopes), acute (exclude neuro), sensory, consecutive, sagging eye (age-related distance ET), cyclic, high-myopia (heavy eye).
points: Microtropia: may not show on cover test; 4 Δ test; treat refraction + amblyopia.
Acute ET ~5–6 yrs: check pupils, discs, nystagmus, 6th nerve; consider imaging.
Sensory ET: dilated fundus exam always (retinoblastoma!).
Consecutive ET after IXT surgery: act within 6 weeks.
Sagging eye: LR–SR band degeneration → distance ET, ptosis, deep sulcus.
High myopia ET: SR nasal, LR inferior → MRI; SR–LR loop (plication).
Cyclic ET: 24-hour on/off.
chunks.hook: New squint in a child → look at the back of the eye.

cards.q: Features of microtropia (monofixation syndrome)?
cards.a: Angle <10 Δ, anisometropia, mild amblyopia, ARC with central suppression scotoma, peripheral fusion, reduced stereo.

cards.q: Cause of age-related distance esotropia (sagging eye)?
cards.a: Degeneration of the LR–SR band letting the LR pulley sag inferiorly.

chunks.title: Exotropias
chunks.tldr: Intermittent XT: ~2 yrs, breaks down with tiredness/daydreaming; closes one eye in bright light. Types: distance excess (true vs simulated), basic, CI. Constant early XT: neuro associations. Sensory XT: poor vision. Consecutive XT: after ET surgery.
points: Simulated distance excess unmasked by +3 D lenses (high AC/A) or 30–60 min patch (tenacious proximal fusion).
Rx: myopic glasses/over-minus, part-time patching, exercises (near).
Surgery if poor/worsening control: unilateral R&R or bilateral LR recession (true distance excess).
Sensory XT: restoring vision may still leave intractable diplopia.
Consecutive XT surgery: 75% aligned at 10 yrs; check diplopia risk; early divergence → slipped muscle?
chunks.hook: Sunshine squint = intermittent exotropia.

cards.q: Classic sign of intermittent exotropia in bright light?
cards.a: Closing one eye.

cards.q: How is simulated distance-excess exotropia unmasked?
cards.a: Re-measure near through +3 D lenses or after 30–60 min monocular occlusion.

chunks.title: Duane retraction syndrome
chunks.tldr: Hypoplastic VI nucleus + LR innervated by III → co-contraction → globe retraction + fissure narrowing on adduction. Type I (commonest): poor abduction. Type II: poor adduction. Type III: both. Face turn keeps BSV. Never resect the LR.
points: Often bilateral; 10% familial; half have systemic defects (deafness, ear, skeletal).
Up-shoot/down-shoot in adduction (tight LR slipping).
Most need no surgery; operate if losing BSV, bad head posture, shoots.
Options: MR/LR recessions; VRT (SR ± IR to LR).
Amblyopia usually from anisometropia.
chunks.hook: Duane Type 1 = can't go Out (1 = abduction). Eye shrinks back when it goes in.

cards.q: Pathogenesis of Duane syndrome?
cards.a: Absent/hypoplastic sixth nerve nucleus with aberrant innervation of LR by third nerve fibres.

cards.q: Most common Huber type?
cards.a: Type I – limited abduction.

chunks.title: Möbius, CFEOM, MED & Brown
chunks.tldr: Möbius: bilateral VI + VII palsy (mask face) ± limb defects. CFEOM1 (KIF21A): ptosis + eyes stuck below horizontal, chin up. MED: can't elevate one eye in any position. Brown: can't elevate in adduction (SO tendon restriction); click.
points: Möbius: also V, VIII, X, XII; horizontal gaze palsy 50%.
Strabismus fixus: eyes tethered in (MR) or out (LR).
Marcus Gunn jaw-wink is a CCDD.
Brown: mild (no hypo), moderate (down-shoot in adduction), severe (primary hypotropia, chin up, face turn away).
Acquired Brown: trauma, RA, sinusitis → steroids near trochlea.
Congenital Brown often improves by ~10 yrs; surgery = SO tendon lengthening.
chunks.hook: Brown = can't look up-and-in (like an IO palsy but forced duction positive).

cards.q: Motility defect in Brown syndrome?
cards.a: Limited elevation in adduction (positive forced duction, SO tendon restriction).

cards.q: Cranial nerves classically affected in Möbius syndrome?
cards.a: Bilateral VI and VII.

chunks.title: A and V patterns
chunks.tldr: V significant ≥15 Δ (more divergent up): IO overaction, SO underaction (infantile ET), 4th palsy, Brown. A significant ≥10 Δ (more divergent down; reading trouble): SO overaction. MR → move to the apex; LR → move to the open end.
points: Also from pulley displacement, craniofacial anomalies.
With oblique dysfunction: V → IO weakening; A → SO posterior tenotomy (~20°) or total tenotomy (up to 50°).
V-ET: MR recess + move down. V-XT: LR recess + move up.
A-ET: MR recess + move up. A-XT: LR recess + move down.
chunks.hook: MR to the Apex (MALE): Medials Apex, Laterals Empty end.

cards.q: Minimum difference for a significant A pattern?
cards.a: 10 Δ (V pattern needs 15 Δ).

cards.q: In V-pattern esotropia, which way are the medial recti transposed?
cards.a: Downward (towards the apex of the V).

chunks.title: Squint surgery procedures
chunks.tldr: Fix glasses + amblyopia first. Strengthen: resection, plication (reversible, spares ciliary vessels), advancement. Weaken: recession (not SO), disinsertion/myectomy (IO), Faden posterior fixation. Transposition for absent muscle (6th palsy). Adjustable sutures for adults (thyroid, blow-out, re-ops).
points: IO recession: reattach 3 mm posterior + temporal to IR temporal insertion edge.
Faden: suture belly ~12 mm behind insertion → weakens only in field of action (convergence excess, DVD with SR).
Adjustables: noose knot, adjust hours later under topical; not for young kids.
Complications: slipped/lost muscle (MR), globe perforation (high myopia), posterior Tenon breach → fat adherence (IO), over/under-correction, anterior segment ischaemia (≤3 recti per eye).
chunks.hook: Never more than 3 recti in one eye (anterior ciliary arteries).

cards.q: Which muscle cannot be recessed?
cards.a: Superior oblique.

cards.q: How to avoid anterior segment ischaemia in squint surgery?
cards.a: Don't operate on more than three rectus muscles of one eye at once (plication spares vessels).

chunks.title: Botulinum toxin in strabismus
chunks.tldr: EMG-guided injection; onset days, peak 1–2 weeks, gone by ~3 months. Muscle lengthens, antagonist shortens → lasting change. Uses: small residual angle, infantile ET, active thyroid, diplopia risk test, BSV potential, 6th palsy (into MR). Side effect: ptosis (16% adults, 25% kids).
points: Best results when fusion stabilises alignment.
Residual ET after recession: inject MR at 2–8 weeks.
Infantile ET: both MRs.
4th palsy: ipsilateral IO or contralateral IR.
Multiple failed operations: repeated injections.
chunks.hook: Botox: 2 weeks to peak, 3 months to fade.

cards.q: Commonest side effect of botulinum for strabismus?
cards.a: Temporary ptosis.

cards.q: Use of botulinum in 6th nerve palsy?
cards.a: Inject the ipsilateral medial rectus to relieve contracture/diplopia and assess LR function.
